title: SYSK Selects: Is Stockholm Syndrome real?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode "Is Stockholm Syndrome Real?" (originally November 2012), introduced by Josh as one of his favorite episodes. The hosts examine Stockholm syndrome: its origin in a 1973 Stockholm bank robbery and the coining of the term by psychologist Nils Bergstrand, the disputed prevalence (including an FBI hostage database), the proposed factors (uneven power, belief escape is impossible, isolation, self-preservation), the stages from obedience to identification with the captor, and cases like Natascha Kampusch, Jaycee Lee Dugard, the TWA hijacking, and Patty Hearst. They note hostage negotiators sometimes encourage it to keep hostages alive. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about flintlock muzzleloader hunting and a plug for a past episode on knife hunting.

segments.title: Opening banter and rerun introduction
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects rerun of 'Is Stockholm Syndrome Real?' and the hosts joke about Chuck's cold and kidnapping.

segments.title: Definition and press coverage
segments.summary: The hosts define Stockholm syndrome as identifying with and feeling empathy for a captor after captivity, discuss how the press sensationalizes it, and compare it to brainwashing.

segments.title: 1973 Stockholm bank robbery origin
segments.summary: The term came from a 1973 bank robbery and hostage standoff in Stockholm, Sweden, in which hostages sided with the captors against police. Psychologist Nils Bergstrand, the police liaison, is usually credited with coining the term.

segments.title: Short versus long-term captivity cases
segments.summary: The hosts debate whether the syndrome forms over short intense periods or long captivity, citing Natascha Kampusch's eight years in a basement, Jaycee Lee Dugard's eighteen years, and the TWA hijacking hostage who called the hijackers not bad people.

segments.title: Factors and stages of Stockholm syndrome
segments.summary: Factors include an uneven power relationship, a belief that escape is impossible, isolation, and a self-preservation instinct. Stages involve obeying the captor, learning their patterns, and responding to minor kindness by seeing the captor as a savior.

segments.title: Prevalence debate and hostage negotiation
segments.summary: Prevalence is debated; an FBI Hostage Barricade Database found little sign of the syndrome, though many cases involve people who already know each other. Hostage negotiators sometimes encourage it because it can keep hostages alive.

segments.title: Patty Hearst case
segments.summary: Patty Hearst, kidnapped by the Symbionese Liberation Army, joined them in a bank robbery, then publicly opposed the group after release; the hosts discuss whether she was faking it and note the Warhol portrait and her later John Waters films.

segments.title: Listener mail: flintlock hunting and knife hunting
segments.summary: A listener describes flintlock muzzleloader hunting with his father, and the hosts reference an older episode on knife hunting. The episode ends with a call for listener stories.
